articles.title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
articles.excerpt: You know that moment when you’re staring at your screen, and you just can’t seem to find the right way to express what you want in code? It’s frustrating, right? Well, I've been diving deep into the w…
articles.body: You know that moment when you’re staring at your screen, and you just can’t seem to find the right way to express what you want in code? It’s frustrating, right? Well, I've been diving deep into the world of AI coding agents, and I can’t help but feel a mix of excitement and skepticism. Sure, these AI tools can churn out lines of code faster than I can finish my morning coffee, but I've noticed something peculiar: they generate a ton of code, but not necessarily more software. Ever wondered why that is? The Promise of AI Coding Agents When I first started experimenting with AI coding agents, I was like a kid in a candy store. With tools like GitHub Copilot and OpenAI Codex offering suggestions and even generating entire functions, it felt like I’d stumbled upon a cheat code for coding.
articles.author: Aman Shekhar

articles.title: 7 Rollback Drills for Junior Developers Comparing Small Business App Logging APIs
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: Run a seven-day rollback evidence drill before choosing between self-hosted Loki and a hosted logging API. Feed both paths the same structured support events, simulate a bad release, and time h…
articles.body: TL;DR: Run a seven-day rollback evidence drill before choosing between self-hosted Loki and a hosted logging API. Feed both paths the same structured support events, simulate a bad release, and time how long a junior developer needs to reconstruct one customer's incident. Pick the operating model that preserves evidence during rollback with fewer unowned chores. Setup speed matters. Recovery clarity matters more. For a small customer-support app, the real question is not which log screen looks friendlier. It is whether the team can prove what happened after application code, log schemas, and deployments have moved on. A quick ingestion setup that loses correlation at the first rollback fails in the only moment that counts.
articles.author: LinusHolm3764

articles.title: Shivacon-Energy: The 0.5B Energy LLM That Refuses to Hallucinate
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: Shivacon-Energy is a LoRA fine-tune of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct for energy-domain Q&A (solar, wind, storage, grids) that passed a brutal 4-gate sellability harness: 9/10 domain tasks, 5/5 unknown-…
articles.body: TL;DR: Shivacon-Energy is a LoRA fine-tune of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct for energy-domain Q&A (solar, wind, storage, grids) that passed a brutal 4-gate sellability harness: 9/10 domain tasks, 5/5 unknown-honesty, 5/5 refusal, 5/5 JSON formatting, 0/10 hallucinations. It was the only survivor of 9 domain adapters trained on a free Colab T4 — and the repo publishes the 8 failures too. Public at Shivay00001/shivacon-energy . The problem it solves Small language models have a specific, expensive failure mode in agentic pipelines: they hallucinate with confidence and they mangle structured output. Most tiny fine-tunes make this worse — the model memorizes narrow patterns, invents facts fluently, and breaks the JSON your tool pipeline depends on.

No markdown fences. That's a prompt written as a type signature.

articles.title: useMemo, React.memo, useRef, and Custom Hooks — Real-World React Guide
articles.excerpt: useMemo caches an expensive calculation, React.memo skips unnecessary component re-renders, useRef stores values without causing re-renders, and custom hooks let you reuse stateful logic across compon…
articles.body: useMemo caches an expensive calculation, React.memo skips unnecessary component re-renders, useRef stores values without causing re-renders, and custom hooks let you reuse stateful logic across components. Together, they make React apps cleaner and faster when used correctly. Quick Difference Tool Main Job Causes Re-render? useMemo Cache a calculated value No React.memo Skip re-render if props do not change No useRef Store mutable value or access DOM No Custom Hook Reuse stateful logic Depends on hooks inside it useMemo memoizes a value, while React.memo memoizes a component. useMemo — Cache Expensive Values useMemo stores the result of a calculation and recalculates it only when its dependencies change. It takes a function and a dependency array.

articles.title: Local-First Sync, Done Right: Inside the SQLite Sync Stack
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: Four open-source Python repositories form a complete local-first synchronization stack: sqlite-sync-core captures SQLite changes as structured operations, packages them into self-contained bund…
articles.body: TL;DR: Four open-source Python repositories form a complete local-first synchronization stack: sqlite-sync-core captures SQLite changes as structured operations, packages them into self-contained bundles, and applies them deterministically across disconnected devices; sqlite-sync-snapshot adds content-addressed snapshot storage; sync-coordination orchestrates nodes with vector clocks and CRDT-style merge; and merkle-dag-store provides the content-addressed block layer underneath. All public under Shivay00001 . The problem it solves Offline-first applications live or die on sync.

articles.excerpt: Using the NASA spacecraft Swift, astronomers observed a supermassive black hole burping radio jets 300 days after a heavy cosmic meal.
articles.body: Using the NASA X-ray spacecraft Swift combined with radio observations, astronomers have observed a supermassive black hole burping radio jets 300 days after a heavy cosmic meal. The team was also able to roughly estimate the mass of this feeding cosmic titan, which sits at the heart of the Perseus Cluster, a massive collection of thousands of galaxies. The black hole sits at the center of the galaxy NGC 1275, located around 225 light-years away, and is the brightest galaxy of the Perseus Cluster . The supermassive black hole first flared in X-rays, which indicated an increase in the rate at which it was accreting matter.

articles.excerpt: NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions.
articles.body: NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions. The agency opened a "Lunar Grounding Challenge" to avoid situations where an astronaut on the moon could become "a walking, high voltage capacitor." Submissions for the $150,000 competition are due Jan. 15 and you can see the requirements here . NASA is hoping to put astronaut boots at the lunar south pole in 2028 during the Artemis 4 or 5 missions, on the first landing mission since NASA's Apollo 17 in 1972. But simulations suggest that both "tribocharging" (electric-charge transfer between two objects) and plasma charging (from ambient gas in the region) could build up electric charge on spacesuits.

articles.body: NASA experiments focused on human and plant health and drug-resistant organisms will travel to the International Space Station aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, advancing research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration. This research supports astronaut health during long-duration missions through four investigations from the agency’s Biological and Physical Sciences division, including 3D models of the human brain, a crop disease study, a faster way to assess astronaut health, and an analysis of antibiotic-resistant bacteria aboard the space station.

articles.title: The 'Halloween Fireballs' are coming. Here's what to expect from the Taurids this year
articles.excerpt: The Southern and Northern Taurid meteor showers will produce occasional bright, slow-moving meteors worldwide during October and November, with moon-free peaks in 2026.
articles.body: They don't produce anything like the torrent of "shooting stars" associated with August's Perseids or December's Geminids, but the Taurid meteor showers have something else going for them — fireballs. The Taurids are famous for occasionally producing exceptionally bright, slow-moving meteors that can streak dramatically across the night sky from September to December. As a bonus, they're visible from both the Northern and Southern hemispheres. That's because they appear to emanate from the constellation Taurus, which sits close to the ecliptic, the apparent path the sun takes across the sky as Earth orbits around it. The Taurids are actually two closely related showers — the Southern Taurids and Northern Taurids — whose activity overlaps in late October and November.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 12, 1964: The Soviet Union launches Voskhod 1, the 1st multi-person cosmonaut crew, into space
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight . This was the first time that a spacecraft carried more than one person into orbit, with three cosmonauts packed inside the spacecraft. Only two cosmonauts were originally supposed to fly on this mission, but Soviet politicians pressured the Russian space program to add one more. This left no room for spacesuits on board, so this also became the first spaceflight without spacesuits . Two of the crewmembers, an engineer and a doctor, became the first civilians to go to space. On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched the first multiperson mission, Voskhod 1, which launched three Russian cosmonauts into space.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

articles.title: Namibian salt flats look like an alien planet | Space photo of the day for Oct. 12, 2026
articles.excerpt: The Etosha Pan in northern Namibia, the largest salt flat in the country, looks otherworldly in this satellite photo.
articles.body: The Etosha Pan, Namibia's largest salt pan, seen from space. (Image credit: Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2026), processed by ESA) A neon blue pool swirls amongst what look like clouds, all surrounded by a bright red stretch of land. This might look like the surface of an alien planet , but it's actually a salt flat right here on Earth , seen from space. What is it? Etosha National Park in northern Namibia hosts the largest salt pan, or piece of land covered with salt and other minerals, in the country. This image of the Etosha Pan was captured on April 5 of this year by Europe's Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission, which consists of two identical satellites in the same orbit.
